# A RESPONSE TO "INSTITUTIONAL LOGIC OF BUSINESS BUBBLES: LESSONS FROM THE DUBAI BUSINESS SCHOOL MANIA." THE DEVELOPMENT OF DUBAI AS A GLOBAL BUSINESS EDUCATION HUB
###### TIM ROGMANS Zayed University, Dubai, United Arab Emirates
As a response to the article by[ Alajoutsijarvi,](#page-7-0) ¨ [Juusola, and Lamberg (2014)](#page-7-0) on "Lessons From the Dubai Business School Mania," this Dialogue contribution applies aspects of International business theory to analyze the development of the business education sector in Dubai and proposes a new classification of business education hubs. I argue that Dubai occupies a unique global position as a result of the highly international nature of both its business schools and its student population. Other business school hubs are either dominated by local universities (e.g., Boston, London) or cater primarily to local students (e.g., Malaysia). This gives rise to the question: "Why do so many business schools and students from around the world meet in Dubai and not elsewhere?" In a manner that is consistent with institutional theory [(North 1991](#page-8-0);[ Kunci](#page-8-0)ˇ [c, 2014](#page-8-0)), I ˇ argue that the international business school sector in Dubai continues to grow primarily as a result of a government strategy to provide a supportive regulatory framework for both universities and students. This strategy was reinforced in 2006 with the establishment of the Knowledge and Human Development Authority (KHDA), a specialist regulatory body for the education sector. Regulations have been developed to attract reputable foreign operators while maintaining quality standards, which in turn attract local and foreign students to study in Dubai. This is an example of the "build it and they will come" strategy that has worked well in different sectors in Dubai, including transport, tourism, and retail. Although the Dubai government has not actually built the business schools that are now operating in the Emirate, it has developed the environment

## LESSONS FROM THE DUBAI BUSINESS SCHOOL MANIA
In their article in the Academy of Management Learning & Education,[ Alajoutsijarvi, Juusola, and](#page-7-0) ¨ [Lamberg (2014)](#page-7-0) address the question "How is it possible that the world's top business schools simultaneously judged the market so badly and collectively invested in activities that, in retrospect, were far from economically rational?" The authors describe the rapid growth of both Dubai itself and the business school sector up to 2008, which ultimately resulted in "the bursting of the bubble, 2009–2012." Justification for referring to this period as "the bursting of the bubble" consists primarily of a description of the fall in Dubai property prices and a general economic slowdown, in combination with the observation that "some schools have gone bankrupt and many others have been forced to exit or downsize." In support, a table shows that during the years 2009–2010, five schools exited the market and no new schools opened during this period.
To explain the rapid growth and subsequent decline of business schools in Dubai, the authors use bubble theory supplemented by an institutional perspective on economic bubbles. Based on [Kindleberger and Aliber (2011)](#page-7-0), a general framework for bubbles is provided, whereby initial growth in a sector is followed by euphoria and mania and in turn by distress, revulsion, and the bursting of the bubble,
leading to "a panic that feeds on itself in a manner similar to the initial speculation" ([Alajoutsijarvi](#page-7-0) ¨ [et al., 2014)](#page-7-0). The authors subsequently draw on institutional perspectives to explain that people construct worldviews, rules, and norms that they share with other similar organizations and individuals [(Lok, 2010)](#page-8-0). It is argued that individuals and organizations can be "susceptible to mimicry or group behavior" [(Alajoutsijarvi et al., 2014)](#page-7-0) and that this ¨ has been a contributing factor to the decisions by business schools to set up in Dubai, especially in a context of administrative professionalization at business schools, with a declining input by faculty members in investment decisions [(Ginsberg, 2011](#page-7-0)). The article concludes that the "business schools made most of the mistakes that are listed in the literature" and that business school leaders need to pay attention to the economic history of the business school industry.
A review of more recent developments of business schools in Dubai demonstrates that it is questionable that there was a bubble that burst in Dubai, in the way prescribed by bubble theory. As reported by[ Alajoutsijarvi et al. (2014)](#page-7-0), of the five business ¨ schools that closed during 2009–2010, two moved to a neighboring Emirate inside the United Arab Emirates (UAE) (Mahatma Gandhi University, Bharati Vidyapeeth University); one closed due to problems at the parent institution (EHSAL); one is still active albeit no longer as a business school (Michigan State University); and one closed due to a dearth of students (PIM, Sri Lanka). All the other 21 business schools examined in the article were open in 2012 and are all still operating as of January 2018 [(KHDA, 2018)](#page-8-0). According to Dubai's Knowledge and Human Development Authority ([KHDA, 2017](#page-7-0)), the total number of Higher Education Providers now stands at 62 in Dubai, including both International Branch Campuses (IBCs) and local universities. The number of universities in Dubai has grown during each of the last 30 years except for 2009–2010, when the number of providers declined by one. Within this group of universities, the number of IBCs has grown from 30 in 2009 to 39 in 2017, again with the only decline taking place in 2009–2010 [(KHDA,](#page-7-0) [2017](#page-7-0)).
[Alajoutsijarvi et al. (2014)](#page-7-0) state that ¨ "after the bubble burst," there was "aggressive competition for a declining number of qualified students." Although it is certainly the case that competition among business school has intensified, the total number of students in Dubai has actually increased each year, even during the 2008–2012 period ([KHDA, 2013](#page-7-0)).
The only recorded reduction in the number of foreign students was in 2010, when their number fell by 682, a fall of less than 3% compared to the previous year. During the same period, the proportion of students taking a business degree and the proportion of students studying at IBCs both increased ([KHDA,](#page-7-0) [2013)](#page-7-0). Although increasing competition between schools has resulted in pressure on business school tuition fees, there is no evidence of any collapse in prices usually witnessed when a bubble bursts. In short, the available data for the 2002–2012 period does not fit the patterns described by bubble theory, with a collapse in new entrants and a proliferation of exits ([Tuckett, 2011](#page-8-0)) leading to a panic that feeds on itself ([Kindleberger & Aliber, 2011)](#page-7-0). In retrospect, when considering the Dubai business school sector during the 2009–2012 period in terms of number of entrants, exits, and students, as well as fee levels, the situation is more akin to a temporary slowdown in growth than the bursting of a bubble.
"When considering the Dubai business school sector during the 2009–2012 period in terms of number of entrants, exits, and students, as well as fee levels, the situation is more akin to a temporary slowdown in growth than the bursting of a bubble."
The authors supplement their argument with an institutional perspective, explaining that organizations within a particular field adopt increasingly similar structures, processes, and rhetoric over time ([Alajoutsijarvi et al., 2014)](#page-7-0). It can indeed be ¨ observed that business schools are following each other to some extent in their internationalization efforts. Certainly, the fact that other business schools are already present in a location can provide comfort to newcomers, and the interview data in the original article supports this perspective. However, the percentage of business schools with an IBC anywhere in the world is still very low. The Observatory of Borderless Higher Education [(Garrett, Kinser, Lane, &Merola, 2016](#page-7-0)) reports a total of 246 IBCs in the world, and these do not all include a business school. According to the[ AACSB (2018)](#page-7-0) there are over 16,000 business schools in the world, so the available data suggests that less than 2% of business schools have opened an IBC. The statement that 10 of the top-100 business schools (Financial Times ranking) have a presence in Dubai [(Alajoutsijarvi et al.,](#page-7-0) ¨ [2014](#page-7-0)) may point to a degree of group behavior among the top schools. It is worth noting that half of these top
schools have a presence in Dubai only in the form of centers where student support is provided, whereby lecturers fly in to give classes to part-time students. Of course, even the choice for this particular mode of operation can be the result of institutional behavior, with top schools mimicking the location and business model choices of others that are already present. Therefore, there is data to support the idea that business schools follow each other when making location decisions, but it is difficult to unambiguously establish to what extent institutional behavior, as opposed to the particular advantages of Dubai as a location, is driving these strategies. Irrespective of the motivational drivers, premier institutions seem to continue to be keen to open in Dubai. During 2017 and 2018, the University of Birmingham and Babson College have announced their plans to open a Dubai campus, and the Rochester Institute of Technology has announced a large expansion plan.
## DEVELOPMENTS 20132018
Recent developments point toward a continuously growing market for Dubai business schools. During the 2013–2016 period, total student numbers in Dubai have increased by 9.6% per annum to over 60,310, and the proportion of all students who are enrolled in a business program has increased from 42 to 52.7% ([KHDA, 2017](#page-7-0)). In this growing market, expatriates account for 56% of Dubai's total student population [(KHDA, 2017](#page-7-0)). In parallel, IBCs have increased their share of the total student population from 42.8% in 2010–2011 to 46% in 2015–2016 ([KHDA, 2017)](#page-7-0), indicating that the number of students at IBCs has grown at an even faster rate than the Dubai university student population overall.
The Observatory on Borderless Higher Education [(Garrett et al., 2016)](#page-7-0) reports that China has now overtaken the UAE as the country with the most IBCs, with China having 32 IBCs, and the UAE hosting 31 IBCs, followed by Singapore and Malaysia with 12 IBCs each. In Dubai, more than half of the IBCs are Anglo Saxon (originating from Australia, the United Kingdom, or the United States), accounting for 73% of the total student population at IBCs and 79% of business students [(KHDA, 2018)](#page-8-0). At the same time, 86% of all students in Dubai originate from Asia and the Middle East North Africa (MENA) region (including the UAE), with most Emirati students attending one of the Federal Institutions of Higher Education
(Zayed University and the Higher Colleges of Technology). The picture that emerges from this analysis is one of Anglo-Saxon IBCs offering business education to foreign students from Asia and theMENA region. A significant but unknown share of these Asian and Arab students are already residents of the UAE before attending university, but increasingly they are choosing to remain in Dubai rather than move to the UK, US, or India for their university studies. At the same time, Asian and Arab youths are coming to Dubai to obtain an Anglo-Saxon business degree relatively close to home. Although detailed statistics on when expatriate students originally entered Dubai are not available, the fact that the Dubai student population has grown by 1.5 times the growth rate of Dubai's overall population indicates that most likely there is an increasing number of students moving to Dubai for their studies. This situation in Dubai is in contrast to IBCs in China, where the target audience is mainly local Chinese students.
"Therefore, there is data to support the idea that business schools follow each other when making location decisions, but it is difficult to unambiguously establish to what extent institutional behavior, as opposed to the particular advantages of Dubai as a location, is driving these strategies."
"The term education hub is a relatively new phenomenon that has not been the subject of much academic research."
## INTERNATIONAL EXPANSION OF BUSINESS SCHOOLS
### Education Hubs and International Branch Campuses
Because Dubai's IBCs cater mostly to foreign students, and business studies is by far the most popular study program ([KHDA, 2017)](#page-7-0), it is clear that Dubai has become an international hub for business education. In the context of the internationalization of research and education, the term education hub is a relatively new phenomenon that has not been the subject of much academic research and has no generally accepted definition.[ Kinser and Lane (2015)](#page-7-0) refer to the term, hub, as an evocative metaphor that
encompasses different types of strategies, usually including the development of private-sector universities and IBCs.[ Knight (2011)](#page-7-0) has offered the following working definition of the term:
An education hub is a planned effort to build a critical mass of local and international actors strategically engaged in education, training, knowledge production, and innovation activities.
[Knight (2011)](#page-7-0) describes the efforts of six countries that have announced plans to position themselves within their region and beyond as education hubs (Singapore, Malaysia, Hong Kong, UAE, Qatar, Bahrain).[ Knight (2011)](#page-7-0) does not address city-level hubs, which might have resulted in the inclusion of cities such as Boston or London in her study. Other research on education hubs include case studies of Asian hubs such as Singapore ([Ho Mok, 2008](#page-7-0)), and Malaysia [(Knight & Morshidi, 2011](#page-7-0)).[ Knight (2015)](#page-7-0) has offered a preliminary classification of education hubs into three types (student hub, education and training hub, knowledge and innovation hub) and acknowledged that more research needs to be done into this relatively recent phenomenon.
A related stream of higher education literature concerns the establishment and management of IBCs.[ Lane (2011a)](#page-8-0) found that IBCs are set up either to provide something different or better than what is already provided or to absorb excess demand in a country. Since IBCs are typically not subsidized by the home institution, they rely on tuition fees, host-government subsidies, and private partner investments as their primary sources of finance [(Lane](#page-8-0) [2011b](#page-8-0)). In the cases of Dubai and Malaysia, the presence of IBCs was intended to create new demand in the local higher education sector, keeping local students from studying abroad and attracting foreign students ([Lane, 2011a)](#page-8-0). Because IBCs entail significant financial and reputational risk for parent institutions, several studies address their riskmanagement aspects [(Wilkins, 2016](#page-8-0);[ Hommel, Li, &](#page-7-0) [Pastwa, 2016)](#page-7-0).[ Lane (2011b)](#page-8-0) identified significant managerial and leadership challenges related to expansion through IBCs.
#### Toward a Classification of Education Hubs
Knight'[s (2015)](#page-7-0) classification of education hubs into three types mentioned above is difficult to test empirically on the basis of the available data. Although local authorities may have ambitions to progress from student hubs to innovation hubs, it is not easy to determine when a location fits one classification
or another. It is even possible that locations become innovation hubs without ever being international student hubs. To complement the tools available to analyze education hubs, I propose to conceptualize a new classification of education destinations along two criteria: the international dimension of its student population and the international dimension of the business schools that are operating in the location. Applying this classification to eight locations (both cities and countries) that are most often referred to as education hubs in the literature, results in Figure 1 below.
The positioning of education hubs in the matrix is schematic and determined by available information on the number of international students as a proportion of total students (for the vertical axis) and an estimate of the capacity of IBCs as a proportion of total capacity of the location's business schools (for the horizontal axis). Not all cities and countries shown in the matrix fit neatly into one of the quadrants, but the position of each location does indicate its characteristics as a hub relative to the other locations shown. In the top-left quadrant, cities such as Boston and London are predominantly supplied by local universities, rather than IBCs. London has a slightly higher number of IBCs than Boston ([Garret](#page-7-0) [et al., 2016)](#page-7-0), but in both cases traditional local universities dominate the supply of higher education. Although the student populations in Boston and London are for the majority composed of local nationals, they both have a significant proportion of

In the bottom-right side of the matrix, Malaysia, Singapore, and Hong Kong are characterized by a strong presence of foreign universities and a largely domestic student population. Even though the number of foreign students is by no means negligible, they are just a small minority of the total student population. Malaysia, in particular, has a significant and growing international population in higher education ([New](#page-8-0) [Straits Times](#page-8-0), 2016), but this still represents less than 15% of the total population of university students in the country. IBCs in China focus even more strongly on local students than those in Malaysia, Singapore, and Hong Kong. In terms of the national origin of business schools, China is the country with the highest number of IBCs in the world, but their local impact is still relatively minor in terms of the share that these IBCs represent in the vast Chinese market for business education. Hence, relative to other education hubs, China is still characterized by a dominance of local suppliers and local students, which results in China's position in the bottom-left quadrant. The growing number of IBCs in China correspond to the description by[ Lane (2011a)](#page-8-0) in that IBCs offer something different or better than what already exists in the local market. Finally, in the top right-hand quadrant, Dubai and Qatar are uniquely characterized as hubs with predominantly foreign students and foreign universities. Although the two locations are in the same quadrant of the matrix, there are important differences in their scale and nature as education hubs. In particular, in terms of numbers of students and universities, the market for international business education ismuch larger in Dubai than in Qatar. Other differences between Dubai and Qatar are further analyzed below.
In summary, Dubai is unique among the business education hubs pictured in[ Figure 1](#page-3-0) in that IBCs and international students in business studies are significant, both in terms of their absolute number and as a proportion of the location's business education market. This analysis of the development of the Dubai business school sector in its global context raises the question as to why so many international universities and students have chosen Dubai as their location to provide and obtain business education.
## International Business Schools and International Business Theory
In "The Competitive Advantage of Nations," [Porter](#page-8-0) [(1990)](#page-8-0) describes the Diamond Model to explain the emergence of clusters as a result of factor conditions,
demand conditions, the presence of related and supporting industries, as well as firm strategy, structure, and rivalry. Even though this model has been used to analyze transnational education in China and Malaysia [(Tsiligiris, 2018](#page-8-0)), the analysis does not extend well to the emergence of Dubai as a global education hub. The initial absence of key factors of production (e.g., qualified faculty), a small local population leading to unfavorable demand conditions and the initial absence of related and supporting industries (e.g., student housing) mean that the Diamond Model does not provide a viable theoretical framework for analyzing the development of Dubai's business education sector. In fact, a comprehensive explanation of Dubai's emergence as a business education hub needs to take into account how this phenomenon occurred despite the initial absence of the conditions outlined in Porter's Diamond Model.
The question of internationalization of business schools can better be addressed through the lens of international business theory, which seeks to explain why companies expand internationally in the way that they do.[ Dunning (1977](#page-7-0),[ 2003)](#page-7-0) articulated the OLI framework, stating that companies will expand abroad if there are Ownership, Location, and Internalization advantages to doing so. In this framework, ownership advantages include the competitive advantages of a firm that will help it to succeed in foreign markets, such as a brand name, proprietary knowledge, or financial resources. International business theory suggests that there is a "liability of foreignness" [(Johanson & Vahlne, 1977)](#page-7-0), which places the foreign investor at a disadvantage compared to local competition and that this disadvantage needs to be compensated for by ownership advantages of the foreign organization.
Second, location advantages help to explainwhy the organization chooses a particular country for its foreign activity. These advantages may include a country's market size, quality of institutions, the rule of law, availability of skilled labor, physical infrastructure, and the like. Finally, Internalization advantages refer to the reasons why a company would carry out international activity itself rather than through a contract with a partner. According to transaction costs theory, this will be the case if the cost of contracting with a local partner is greater than controlling the international activity through the organization's internal hierarchy [(Hymer, 1960](#page-7-0)). Transaction costs include the efforts required to identify and monitor foreign partners, which are particularly high if there is the possibility for opportunism (or cheating) on the side of
the local partner ([Williamson, 1985](#page-8-0)). In education, such opportunism may consist of a local partner not adhering to the quality standards stipulated by the parent institution, thereby causing reputational damage. Internalization advantages help to explain the ownership mode an organization chooses for its international activity, ranging from high to low levels of investment and control (i.e., full ownership, joint ventures, licensing, and franchising). They do not address the question of why business activity takes place in a particular location. Hence, in terms of the OLI framework, the remainder of this section will not include a further analysis of internalization advantages, but will focus on ownership and location advantages exclusively. It is sufficient to note at this point that international business schools in Dubai exist along the entire spectrum of ownership options, ranging from full ownership to joint ventures to licensing.
Dunning positioned OLI as a general framework within which to develop theory, rather than as a specific theory of internationalization. In response to criticism that the OLI framework contains so many potential explanatory variables that its predictive value is nearly zero,[ Dunning (2003)](#page-7-0) argued that "the purpose of the eclectic paradigm is not to offer a full explanation of all kinds of international production but rather to point to amethodology and to a generic set of variables which contain the ingredients necessary for any satisfactory explanation of particular types of foreign value-added activity." Within this context, OLI remains the dominant theoretical framework for analyzing the internationalization of companies. Although higher education providers are in most cases not organized as companies, theirinternational expansion is usually set up along the lines of a private-sector initiative with the aim to earn a profit for the parent institution being at least one of themotives [(Lane, 2011a](#page-8-0)). Hence, it is reasonable to build theory on the phenomena of IBCs and education hubs by using aspects of International business theory. In this particular case, "what are the ownership and location advantages that help to explain why international business schools and students are meeting in Dubai and not to the same extent elsewhere?"
In terms of ownership advantages, it is noteworthy that the IBCs operating in Dubai are mostly from Anglo-Saxon countries (Australia, United Kingdom, and United States). These universities draw heavily on their history, brand name, reputation, ranking, and country of origin when marketing to potential students, for example through advertisements in newspapers and on the radio, as well as through university websites and socialmedia. Several Indian and Pakistani
IBCs in Dubai also leverage their brand name built up in their home country to provide business education to Indian and Pakistani residents in Dubai. Additional ownership advantages for IBCs may lie in their experience and knowledge of managing business education. Some business schools are even turning their ability to operate IBCs globally into a source of competitive advantage (e.g., Heriot Watt University, Manipal). However, the aspect of accumulated international experience is likely to be a relatively minor ownership advantage in this context, given the fact that for nearly all IBCs in Dubai, their Dubai operation is their only or first international venture. The presence of financial resources may also be an ownership advantage for business schools looking to expand abroad, but it is noteworthy that the business schools expanding abroad are not typically those with the largest endowments. Indeed, the ability to generate funds to finance academic research activities at home is a prime motivator for business schools to expand abroad [(Garrett et al., 2016](#page-7-0)).
"[W]hat are the ownership and location advantages that help to explain why international business schools and students are meeting in Dubai and not to the same extent elsewhere?"
Location advantages provide an explanation why business schools with international ambitions have chosen Dubai as a place to operate, rather than elsewhere. If the existing population of Dubai (3 million people) is considered as the market size, then the market appears heavily oversupplied. However, considering the international profile of the student body of IBCs, it is clear that IBCs target the whole of the MENASA region (Middle East North Africa South Asia) and beyond for student recruitment. Dubai's success in attracting IBCs and international students is in many ways similar to its success in becoming a business hub in other sectors: quality of life, an excellent physical infrastructurewith easy connections to anywhere in the region and beyond, a safe environment, the availability of land for construction, and the application of rule of law [(Rogmans, 2012](#page-8-0)). The combination of these location advantages can be summarized in the term "infrastructure," which comprises elements of both hard and soft infrastructure. The term soft infrastructure is closely related to the concept of institutional quality, which encompasses the formal and informal "rules of the game" and their enforcement characteristics [(North](#page-8-0) [1991; Kunci](#page-8-0)ˇ c[, 2014](#page-8-0)). Measures of institutional quality ˇ
typically include characteristics along legal, political, and economic dimensions, such as judicial independence, the absence of corruption, quality of a country's bureaucracy, protection of property rights, and absence of capital controls.[ Kunci](#page-8-0)ˇ [c (2014)](#page-8-0) placed ˇ the UAE in the middle tier of a ranking of 197 countries based on institutional quality, noting the country's rapid progress since the 1990s. Among the various rankings of institutional quality and competitiveness, the UAE typically ranks first in the Arab world. However, such general rankings on institutional quality or other rankings of countries' general business environment fail to explain Dubai's unique performance globally in attracting international business schools and students. There are particular institutional characteristics that account for the attractiveness of Dubai as an education destination which are encapsulated by the establishment of Dubai's Knowledge and Human Development Authority (KHDA) in 2006. The KHDA is a regulatory body set up by the Emirate of Dubai with one of its founding objectives listed as "the attraction of private educational institutions, research and studies centres, and reputed international human resources development institutions to establish branches in the Emirate" ([KHDA, 2006](#page-7-0)). The KHDA is a specialist regulator for the education sector in Dubai, providing a clear framework for qualified international business schools to set up in Dubai, while safeguarding the investment that students make when embarking on a degree. The involvement of the KHDA starts at the initial orientation business schools carry out when deciding on international expansion, continues through the licensing process, and runs through to Quality Assurance [(KHDA, 2017](#page-7-0)). Since the establishment of the KHDA in 2006, the number of IBCs in Dubai has nearly tripled, from 11 to 32 [(Garret et al., 2016)](#page-7-0). Although there are risks involved in one organization assuming the dual role of regulator and facilitator, the regulatory role appears to be implemented in a stringent manner, with a significant number of applications rejected [(Alajoutsijarvi et al., 2014)](#page-7-0). ¨
Dubai's strategy and growth are in contrast to Qatar, which is the only other significant example in[ Figure 1](#page-3-0) of a hub with both predominantly international universities and international students. On the one hand, Dubai has focused on creating the right conditions for business schools to set up and then provides support to universities that are considering entry into the Dubai market through the licensing and establishment process. In contrast, Qatar's foreign universities are for the most part based in Education City, a cluster that has developed on the basis of a small number of elite international universities specializing in different
academic disciplines. The universities in Education City have been invited to establish a campus and are financially supported by the government through the Qatar Foundation. In this sense, the role of local authorities is more akin to that of a client than that of a regulator and facilitator. Among the universities in Education City, only HEC and Carnegie Mellon offer business degrees (Education City, 2018). Outside Education City, there are only three foreign universities offering business degrees in Qatar (University of Aberdeen, Stenden University Qatar, College of North Atlantic). The key difference in approach between Dubai and Qatar is between establishing the right conditions for international business schools to set up and flourish (Dubai) versus the government partnering with a small number of elite universities in specific disciplines (Qatar).
Hence, the development of Dubai's business education landscape is not due primarily to general infrastructure or institutional characteristics, although these may have played a role, nor a result of the government reaching out to a small number of highprofile universities, but rather a consequence of an institutional context designed purposefully and specifically for the higher education sector by the Dubai government through the establishment of the KHDA. In terms of the dimensions of the matrix in [Figure 1,](#page-3-0) in the absence of direct financial government support for universities and students from abroad, the greater the international element of an education hub's universities and student population is, the greater the importance of the credibility of the location's institutional arrangements that are required to overcome the liability of foreignness for both universities and students will be.
## CONCLUSIONS
This Dialogue contribution has revisited the contribution by[ Alajoutsijarvi et al. (2014)](#page-7-0) that analyzed ¨ the development of the Dubai business school sector using bubble theory supplemented by an institutional perspective. The argument has been made that the temporary slowdown in growth in the sector does not correspond to the bursting of a bubble in the way that bubble theory suggests. Business schools probably have shown some of the mimicking behaviors described in the original article as institutional theory, with some business schools drawing comfort from the fact that others have gone before, but more empirical evidence is needed to conclude whether this is a more important element than the existing location advantages.
This Dialogue makes a contribution to the literature on the internalization of business education by identifying, describing, and explaining a new phenomenon: the education hub, comprised of predominantly foreign universities and foreign students. An analysis that applies aspects of International business theory to understand the development of the Dubai business education sector as a global hub, points to Dubai being a location where international business schools have chosen to leverage their reputational assets in a supportive and coherent institutional environment. In turn, international studentshave come toDubai because of the large offer of reputable business schools, again supported in their decision making by the credible regulatory environment. For both parties (universities and students), the other hard and soft elements of Dubai's infrastructure provide further support for their choice.
As the business education market continues to internationalize, universities can use the elements of International business theory applied here to support their own international location decision making and on appropriate ownership structures for their international activities. Locations looking to expand their roles as international hubs of business education can use the classification of education hubs developed in this article to position their own activities and formulate their strategies. As demonstrated by Dubai's development, universities' brand image and a specific and effectively enforced regulatory framework for international educational institutions are likely to be the two main driving factors that will shape the growth of international business education.
International branch campuses and global business education hubs are relatively recent phenomena. Existing theory can provide tools to analyze and understand these developments, but new theoretical frameworks and conceptualizations are likely to emerge as well. As a first step, further research within the OLI framework can test in further detail the motivations and drivers of the international expansion decisions of business schools as well as the factors that determine choices on the location and ownership structure of foreign operations.
